title: A tour of the body: cells, tissues, organs, systems

hero.headline: Thirty trillion cells, four tissues, eleven systems: how a body is built, and how we found out

prequestions.prompt: Guess: roughly how many human cells are in an adult man's body?
prequestions.explanation: About 30 to 37 trillion, depending on the study. The old textbook figure of 100 trillion was never measured.

prequestions.prompt: Guess: what share of your human cells, by count, are red blood cells?
prequestions.explanation: About 84%. They are tiny, so they make up only a small share of your mass.

prequestions.prompt: Guess: how many of your cells are replaced each day?
prequestions.explanation: About 330 billion, roughly 80 grams, mostly blood cells and gut lining.

prequestions.prompt: True or false: a newborn baby has more bones than an adult.
prequestions.explanation: True. A newborn has about 270 to 300 separate pieces, which fuse into 206.

prequestions.prompt: Guess: which part of the brain holds most of its neurons?
prequestions.explanation: The cerebellum at the back holds about 69 of the brain's 86 billion neurons.

sections.title: The body that rebuilds itself while you read
sections.intro_md:
In the next sixty seconds your body will make roughly **230 million** new cells and lose about as many. Over a day that comes to about **330 billion** cells, close to **80 grams** of you, swapped out and replaced. Almost nine in ten of them are blood cells. Most of the rest come from the lining of your gut, which is scraped off and rebuilt every few days.

Yet some parts of you hardly change at all. The neurons in your cerebral cortex and the cells in the core of your eye lens are, as far as anyone can measure, as old as you are. So you are both a river and a rock: a fast-flowing current of short-lived cells held in place by a scaffold of long-lived ones.

This day is a tour of that structure, from the smallest living unit up. Cells build **tissues**. Tissues build **organs**. Organs work together as **systems**. Keep that ladder in mind and almost everything in a biology textbook has a place to hang.

data.lifespan: Less than a day to a few days
Fewer than half replaced in a lifetime

spotlights.name: Daily cell turnover
spotlights.spot_it: Not something you can see: a number. About 330 billion cells a day, almost all of them blood and gut lining.
spotlights.story_md: In 2021 Ron Sender and Ron Milo at the Weizmann Institute added up how fast every cell type in a 70 kg reference man dies and is replaced. Their answer: about **0.33 trillion cells a day**, or roughly **3.8 million every second**, weighing about **80 grams**. By number, red blood cells dominate, because there are so many of them and each lives only about four months. By mass, blood cells and the lining of the gut lead. The famous line that "every cell in your body is replaced every seven years" does not survive this kind of accounting. Some tissues are rebuilt in days. Others, such as most neurons, are never replaced.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the body as a process, not an object.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every second, about four million of you quietly retire.

spotlights.name: Dating cells with bomb carbon
spotlights.spot_it: Not visible: carbon-14 from 1950s nuclear tests, locked into DNA the day a cell was born.
spotlights.story_md: Above-ground nuclear tests in the 1950s and early 1960s doubled the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere. After the 1963 test ban treaty it fell steadily, year by year. Every cell that divides copies its DNA from carbon in the food you ate that year, so the DNA carries a date stamp. In **2005** Kirsty Spalding and Jonas Frisen in Stockholm used this to work out the age of human cells taken after death. Gut cells were young. Neurons in the cortex were as old as the person. Later work with the same method showed that fat cells turn over about **10% a year** and heart muscle cells about **1% a year** at age 25, falling with age.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Cold War accident became the best clock biology has.
spotlights.memory_hook: The bomb left a birth date in every cell that was born after it.

sections.title: The body by numbers
sections.intro_md:
Before the tour, a map. The human body has a ladder of organisation: **atoms, molecules, organelles, cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism.** Each rung does something the rung below cannot. A single heart muscle cell twitches. Millions wired together in a tissue beat in step. The heart, an organ made of muscle, connective tissue, nerves and lining, pumps. The circulatory system, heart plus vessels plus blood, keeps every other cell alive.

There are **four basic tissue types** (epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous) and, by the usual textbook count, **11 organ systems**. How many organs there are depends on who is counting: 78 is the most quoted figure, but it is a convention, not a law. Below are the numbers worth carrying in your head. Several of them were revised in the last fifteen years, which is itself a lesson: even the body's basic inventory is still being audited.

data.label: Bacteria
data.note: Roughly 1.3 per human cell, about 200 g

data.label: Bones
data.note: Adult; a newborn has about 270 to 300 pieces

spotlights.name: How many cells are you?
spotlights.spot_it: A blood smear: almost everything you see is a red blood cell, and so, by count, is most of you.
spotlights.story_md: For decades textbooks said 10 trillion, then 100 trillion, with no clear method behind either. In **2013** an Italian team led by Eva Bianconi went organ by organ and reached **37.2 trillion**. In **2016** Sender, Fuchs and Milo reworked the sums for a 70 kg man and got about **30 trillion**, of which roughly **25 trillion are red blood cells**. A **2023** study by Ian Hatton and colleagues estimated about **36 trillion** for a man, **28 trillion** for a woman and **17 trillion** for a ten-year-old. It also found a twist: the small cells win on count, but the big ones, muscle fibres and fat cells, make up most of the mass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of your cells are tiny oxygen carriers; most of your weight sits in a few big cells.
spotlights.memory_hook: Count your cells and you are mostly red blood cells.

spotlights.name: The 1:1 microbe ratio
spotlights.spot_it: Rod-shaped bacteria under an electron microscope, the kind that crowd your colon.
spotlights.story_md: For forty years, talks and textbooks repeated that bacteria outnumber your own cells **ten to one**. The figure came from a rough 1972 estimate by Thomas Luckey that was never meant as a census. The **2016** recount found about **38 trillion bacteria** in a reference man, almost all in the colon, against about **30 trillion human cells**: a ratio of roughly **1.3 to 1**. Together they weigh about **200 grams**. One good bowel movement can shift the ratio in favour of the human side. The microbes still matter: they digest fibre you cannot, make some vitamins, and train the immune system.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A famous number was off by nearly ten times, and nobody checked for decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not 10 to 1. More like 1 to 1, and you flush part of the difference.

sections.title: How we learned what is inside
sections.intro_md:
For most of history, looking inside a human body was forbidden, dangerous or both. **Galen**, the Greek physician in second-century Rome, wrote the anatomy that Europe and the Islamic world followed for 1,300 years, yet he dissected mostly monkeys and pigs. In India, the **Sushruta Samhita** told students to study a corpse layer by layer. Islamic scholars such as **Ibn al-Nafis** in thirteenth-century Cairo questioned Galen on how blood crosses the lungs.

The break came with printing and dissection. **Andreas Vesalius** published his illustrated *Fabrica* in **1543**. **William Harvey** showed in **1628** that blood circulates. Then came the microscope: **Robert Hooke** named the "cell" in **1665**, and **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** saw red blood cells and sperm. By **1839** Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann argued that all living things are made of cells, and in **1855** Rudolf Virchow added that every cell comes from another cell. **Camillo Golgi** and **Santiago Ramon y Cajal** then stained and drew the brain's wiring. Each step needed a new tool or a new permission to look.

spotlights.name: Galen of Pergamon
spotlights.spot_it: Usually shown as a bearded Greek scholar in later European prints; no portrait from life survives.
spotlights.story_md: Galen began as a physician to gladiators in Pergamon, where wounds gave him a window into living bodies. In Rome he became doctor to emperors and wrote so much that his surviving work fills about **20,000 pages**. Human dissection was not allowed, so he cut open **Barbary macaques**, pigs and other animals and assumed humans matched. Some errors followed: a five-lobed liver and a network of vessels at the base of the brain, the rete mirabile, that humans do not have. His authority was so complete that for centuries teachers who found a difference blamed the corpse, not Galen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows how a brilliant authority can freeze a field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Galen anatomised monkeys, and Europe believed him for 1,300 years.

spotlights.name: De humani corporis fabrica
spotlights.spot_it: Full-page woodcuts of flayed men posing in Italian landscapes, muscles peeled back layer by layer.
spotlights.story_md: **Andreas Vesalius** was 28 when his seven-volume *Fabrica* came out in Basel in **1543**, the same year Copernicus published on the heavens. He dissected human bodies himself, at a time when professors read from Galen while a barber did the cutting, and he listed more than **200 errors** in Galen. The woodcuts, probably made in Titian's workshop in Venice, show skeletons leaning on tombs and "muscle men" striding across hills near Padua. If you line up the backgrounds of the muscle plates in order they form a single continuous landscape. The book made anatomy something you check with your own eyes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It founded modern anatomy on observation, not authority.
spotlights.memory_hook: Line up the muscle men and they walk through one Italian landscape.

spotlights.name: William Harvey and the circulation
spotlights.spot_it: The famous figure from his book: a bandaged forearm with swollen veins and a finger pressing one closed.
spotlights.story_md: Galen taught that the liver made blood from food and the body used it up. **William Harvey**, physician to King James I, did the arithmetic. If the heart pushes out even a small amount with each beat, it pumps more blood in an hour than a person weighs. That much could not be made and consumed. It had to go round. In *De motu cordis* (**1628**) he showed it with a tied arm: press a vein and blood refills it only from the side away from the heart, because valves let it flow one way. He could not see the link between arteries and veins. Marcello Malpighi found the capillaries in **1661**, four years after Harvey died.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A sum and a tied arm overturned 1,400 years of medicine.
spotlights.memory_hook: Harvey did the maths: blood must go round.

spotlights.name: Hooke's cork cells
spotlights.spot_it: An engraving of thin cork slices showing rows of empty boxes, like a honeycomb.
spotlights.story_md: **Robert Hooke** published *Micrographia* in **1665**, the first bestseller of science, with huge fold-out engravings of a flea and a louse. Samuel Pepys sat up until 2 am reading it. Looking at a thin slice of cork, Hooke saw tiny empty compartments and called them **cells**, from the Latin *cella*, a small room, because they reminded him of monks' cells. He was looking at the dead walls of plant cells, not at anything alive. The word stuck, and was later applied to the living units that make up every plant and animal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave biology its basic word.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cell was first a monk's small room in a slice of cork.

spotlights.name: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny brass plate the size of a thumb with a single bead of glass in it: his microscope.
spotlights.story_md: Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant in Delft with no university training. He ground single lenses so well that his hand-held microscopes magnified about **270 times**, far beyond the compound microscopes of his day. He sent his findings as letters to the Royal Society in London: blood corpuscles, now called red blood cells, and in **1677** human sperm cells, which he called animalcules. He also scraped plaque from his teeth and saw bacteria swimming in it. He kept his lens-making method secret, and it took others more than a century to match it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was the first person to see single living cells and microbes.
spotlights.memory_hook: A draper with a glass bead saw the first bacteria in his own mouth.

spotlights.name: Cell theory
spotlights.spot_it: Three short rules: every living thing is made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, every cell comes from a cell.
spotlights.story_md: Over dinner in Berlin in **1837**, the botanist **Matthias Schleiden** described plant cell nuclei to the zoologist **Theodor Schwann**. Schwann realised he had seen the same structures in animal tissue. In **1839** he argued that animals, like plants, are built from cells. They had one thing wrong: they thought cells could form by crystallising out of fluid. In **1855** the pathologist **Rudolf Virchow** made famous the Latin phrase *omnis cellula e cellula*, every cell from a cell, an idea Robert Remak had published earlier. It changed medicine: disease, Virchow argued, was cells going wrong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every page of biology since rests on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Omnis cellula e cellula: no cell comes from nothing.

spotlights.name: Golgi, Cajal and the neuron
spotlights.spot_it: Pen-and-ink drawings of single nerve cells with branching trees of dendrites, black on cream paper.
spotlights.story_md: In **1873** the Italian **Camillo Golgi** found a stain, the "black reaction", that coloured only a few nerve cells in a slice, but coloured each one completely. The Spaniard **Santiago Ramon y Cajal** used it and drew what he saw, nearly 3,000 drawings. He argued that the brain is made of separate cells, neurons, that touch without fusing. Golgi believed the opposite, that nerves form one continuous net. They shared the **1906** Nobel Prize and used their lectures to disagree with each other. Electron microscopes in the 1950s showed the gap between neurons, the synapse. Cajal was right.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It founded neuroscience on the single neuron.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two rivals shared a Nobel and argued from the same stage.

sections.title: Inside one cell
sections.intro_md:
A typical human cell is about **10 to 30 micrometres** across. Ten of them in a row would fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence. Inside, it works like a walled town. The **membrane** is the wall, a film of fat two molecules thick that lets some things through and keeps others out. The **nucleus** holds the plans: about **2 metres** of DNA, folded into a space a few millionths of a metre wide. **Ribosomes** read copies of the plans and build proteins. **Mitochondria** turn food and oxygen into ATP, the energy currency every process spends.

But "typical" hides huge range. A red blood cell has thrown out its nucleus. An egg is visible to the naked eye. A single neuron can run from your spine to your big toe. There are hundreds of cell types, and the Human Cell Atlas is still finding new ones. Below are the cells worth knowing by sight.

visual.title: Who makes up your 30 trillion cells (by count, approximate)

spotlights.name: Mitochondrion
spotlights.when: Captured about 1.5 to 2 billion years ago
spotlights.spot_it: In an electron micrograph: a bean-shaped capsule with inner folds like a stack of shelves.
spotlights.story_md: Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. Somewhere around **1.5 to 2 billion years ago** one was swallowed by another cell and, instead of being digested, stayed. They still have their own small loop of DNA, **16,569 letters** and **37 genes**, and they divide on their own inside your cells. Because sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilisation, you inherit yours almost entirely from your mother. A heart muscle cell can hold thousands of them, packed between the fibres, because it never rests. Together they make roughly your body weight in ATP every day, recycling the same molecules over and over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every breath you take is for them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your power stations are tamed bacteria, inherited from your mother.

spotlights.name: Red blood cell
spotlights.spot_it: A red disc dimpled on both sides, like a doughnut with no hole, about 7 to 8 micrometres wide.
spotlights.story_md: A red blood cell gives up its nucleus as it matures, to make room for about **270 million** molecules of haemoglobin, the iron protein that carries oxygen. With no nucleus it cannot repair itself, so it lives only about **120 days** and travels the whole circuit of the body roughly every minute. It is wider than the narrowest capillaries, so it folds to squeeze through in single file. Your bone marrow replaces them at about **2 million a second**. Old ones are broken down in the spleen and liver, and the iron is recycled. The yellow of a fading bruise and the brown of faeces both come from that recycling.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Oxygen delivery to every cell depends on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A disc with no nucleus, squeezing through pipes narrower than itself.

spotlights.name: Neuron
spotlights.spot_it: A cell body with a bushy crown of dendrites and one long tail, the axon.
spotlights.story_md: A neuron collects signals through its branching **dendrites** and sends its own down a single **axon**. Some axons are less than a millimetre long. The ones that run from your lower spine to the muscles of your foot are about **a metre** long, making them among the longest cells in the body. Wrapped in fatty myelin, the fastest fibres carry signals at up to about **120 metres a second**, roughly 430 km an hour. Signals between neurons cross a tiny gap, the synapse, as chemicals. Most neurons in your cortex are never replaced, which is why brain injury is so hard to recover from.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every thought and movement runs on them.
spotlights.memory_hook: One cell can stretch from your spine to your toe.

spotlights.name: Egg and sperm
spotlights.spot_it: A huge round egg surrounded by a crowd of tiny tadpole-shaped sperm, as in a fertilisation photo.
spotlights.story_md: The human egg is the largest cell in the body, about **0.1 millimetres** across, just at the limit of what an eye can see. The sperm is among the smallest: a head about **5 micrometres** long and a tail that drives it. A single ejaculation can hold well over **100 million** sperm, and only one gets in. When it does, the egg's surface changes within seconds to block the rest. From that one fertilised cell come all **30 trillion** cells of an adult, through about 45 rounds of doubling if every cell divided in step, which they do not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every body on Earth started as one cell.
spotlights.memory_hook: The biggest cell meets one of the smallest, and the rest is you.

spotlights.name: Stem cells
spotlights.spot_it: A tight, rounded colony of small cells in a dish, the classic look of embryonic stem cells.
spotlights.story_md: A stem cell can divide to make more of itself and also make specialised cells. The earliest embryo's cells can become anything. Adults keep narrower stem cells, in the bone marrow, the gut lining and the skin, which is how those tissues rebuild so fast. In **2006** Shinya Yamanaka in Kyoto showed that adding just **four genes** to an ordinary skin cell from a mouse could turn it back into a stem-like cell, an **induced pluripotent stem cell**. Human cells followed in 2007, and he shared the **2012** Nobel Prize. A bone marrow transplant, used for leukaemia since the 1950s and 1960s, is the oldest stem cell therapy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Stem cells are why you heal at all.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four genes can wind a skin cell's clock back to the start.

spotlights.name: HeLa cells and Henrietta Lacks
spotlights.spot_it: Glowing cells in a fluorescence image, nuclei blue, the most used human cell line in the world.
spotlights.story_md: In **1951** doctors at Johns Hopkins Hospital took a sample of a cervical tumour from **Henrietta Lacks**, a 30-year-old Black tobacco farmer and mother of five, without asking her. She died that October. Her cells, named **HeLa**, did something no human cells had done before: they kept dividing in a dish, indefinitely. They were used to test the polio vaccine, flown into space, and appear in tens of thousands of studies. Her family learned decades later. In **2023** they reached a settlement with Thermo Fisher Scientific, a company that sold the cells.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Modern cell biology runs on one woman's cells, taken without consent.
spotlights.memory_hook: One woman's cells are still dividing seventy years after her death.

sections.title: Four fabrics: the tissues
sections.intro_md:
Cells of the same kind, working together with the material between them, make a **tissue**. Despite hundreds of cell types, there are only **four basic tissues**, and every organ is a mix of them.

**Epithelial tissue** covers and lines: skin, the inside of the gut, the walls of the lungs' air sacs. Its cells sit tight together on one side of a thin base sheet. **Connective tissue** supports and binds, and it is defined by what lies between its cells: bone is hard mineral, cartilage is rubbery gel, blood is liquid plasma, fat is stored oil, tendon is rope-like collagen. **Muscle tissue** contracts, and comes in three forms. **Nervous tissue** carries signals, made of neurons and their support cells, the glia.

The study of tissues under a microscope is called **histology**. A pathologist reading a biopsy is reading tissue the way you read a page: is the pattern right, or has it gone wrong?

rows.Skeletal muscle: Long striped fibres, many nuclei at the edge
rows.Heart muscle: Striped, branched cells, joined end to end
About 1% a year at 25, less later

spotlights.name: Epithelium
spotlights.spot_it: Under the microscope: a neat sheet of tightly packed cells, sometimes stacked in layers that flatten towards the surface.
spotlights.story_md: Epithelium is the body's wrapping paper and wallpaper. The outer skin is a **stratified** epithelium: new cells are born at the bottom layer and pushed up over about a month, filling with the tough protein keratin and dying before they reach the surface, where they flake off as dust. The gut lining is a single layer that is rebuilt every **3 to 5 days**, because it lives in acid, enzymes and bacteria. The air sacs of the lung are lined by cells so thin that oxygen crosses them in a fraction of a second. Most cancers, carcinomas, start in epithelial tissue, partly because these cells divide so often.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the border between you and the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your skin's surface is a wall of dead cells, rebuilt monthly from below.

spotlights.name: Bone tissue and the osteon
spotlights.spot_it: In cross-section: rings of hard tissue around a central canal, like the growth rings of a tiny tree.
spotlights.story_md: Bone is living connective tissue: collagen fibres hardened with calcium phosphate crystals. The collagen gives it flex, the mineral gives it stiffness, and together they resist both bending and crushing. Dense bone is built from **osteons**, cylinders about 0.2 mm wide, each with a blood vessel down the middle and bone cells trapped in tiny spaces in the rings. Cells called **osteoclasts** dissolve old bone while **osteoblasts** lay down new, so an adult skeleton is replaced at roughly **10% a year**. That is why bones heal, why astronauts lose bone in weightlessness, and why exercise makes them denser.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bone is alive, and it reshapes itself to the loads you put on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your skeleton is quietly dismantled and rebuilt about once a decade.

spotlights.name: Three kinds of muscle
spotlights.spot_it: Stripes say skeletal or heart; no stripes and spindle-shaped cells say smooth muscle.
spotlights.story_md: **Skeletal muscle** moves your bones on command. Its cells are fused into long fibres, some running the whole length of a muscle, each with hundreds of nuclei, and banded with stripes where protein filaments overlap and slide. **Cardiac muscle** is striped too, but its cells branch and lock together with special junctions so a wave of contraction spreads through the heart. **Smooth muscle** has no stripes. It lines the gut, blood vessels, bladder and airways and contracts slowly without you thinking about it. The body has somewhere between **600 and 840** skeletal muscles, depending on how anatomists split them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every movement, from a heartbeat to a swallow, uses one of the three.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stripes for will and heart; smooth for everything that works on its own.

compare.difference: Smooth muscle has no stripes and works without conscious control.

sections.title: From organs to systems
sections.intro_md:
An **organ** is a structure built from at least two tissue types that does a defined job. The stomach has an epithelial lining, smooth muscle walls, connective tissue and nerves. An **organ system** is a team of organs: the stomach works with the mouth, oesophagus, intestines, liver and pancreas as the digestive system.

Textbooks usually list **11 systems**: integumentary (skin, hair, nails), skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, circulatory, lymphatic and immune, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive. The borders are fuzzy. The pancreas sits in two systems at once. The immune system has no single home. And the list of organs keeps moving: in the last decade scientists have argued for adding the mesentery, the interstitium and a pair of salivary glands behind the nose.

data.main parts: Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, white cells

data.job: Filter blood, balance water and salt

spotlights.name: Skin, the largest organ
spotlights.spot_it: Look at the back of your hand: fine lines, pores, hair, and a surface that is entirely dead cells.
spotlights.story_md: Skin covers about **1.5 to 2 square metres** in an adult and is the heaviest single organ. It has three layers: the **epidermis** of dead and dying cells on top, the **dermis** of collagen, blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands and hair roots beneath, and a fatty layer below that. It keeps water in and microbes out, makes vitamin D in sunlight, and cools you with up to several litres of sweat a day in heat. Your fingertips hold thousands of touch sensors per square centimetre. Fingerprint ridges form in the womb around the third and fourth months and never change pattern.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the organ that keeps the inside inside.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your largest organ is mostly dead on the outside.

spotlights.name: Newly named organs
spotlights.spot_it: No single look: a fold of gut tissue, a fluid-filled mesh under the skin, a pair of glands behind the nose.
spotlights.story_md: Three recent claims show how slippery the word "organ" is. In **2016** J. Calvin Coffey in Limerick argued that the **mesentery**, the fold that ties the intestines to the back of the abdomen, is one continuous structure and should count as an organ; many anatomy texts now agree. In **2018** a New York team described the **interstitium**, fluid-filled spaces in a collagen mesh under the skin and around organs, and called it a possible new organ. Many anatomists were unconvinced. In **2020** Dutch radiologists spotted a pair of **tubarial salivary glands** on cancer scans, about **4 cm** long, behind the nose. Others argue they were already described as minor glands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An organ is a definition, and definitions change.
spotlights.memory_hook: The body is still getting new organs, at least on paper.

sections.title: The frame: bones and muscles
sections.intro_md:
The skeleton is not a coat hanger. It protects the brain, heart and lungs, stores calcium and phosphate, and inside the long bones and the pelvis its **marrow** makes about **2 million red blood cells every second**. It also acts as a set of levers for the muscles, which can only pull, never push. That is why muscles work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow, the triceps straightens it.

An adult has **206 bones**. A newborn has about **270 to 300** separate pieces, many of them still partly cartilage. Over childhood they fuse: the skull plates close, the five vertebrae at the base of the spine become one sacrum. Muscles make up roughly **40%** of body weight in a lean adult man and somewhat less in a woman, and they are the body's main furnace: shivering is just muscle burning fuel to make heat.

spotlights.name: The human skeleton
spotlights.spot_it: An upright frame: a skull on a column of 33 vertebrae, a cage of 24 ribs, and long limb bones.
spotlights.story_md: More than half your 206 bones are in your hands and feet: **27** in each hand and **26** in each foot. The spine has **33** vertebrae at birth but fewer separate ones in an adult because the lowest ones fuse. You have **12 pairs** of ribs regardless of sex, despite an old belief that men have one fewer. The only bone that does not touch another bone is the **hyoid**, a U-shaped bone in the neck that anchors the tongue. Ancient Indian surgeons in the Sushruta Samhita counted **300** bones, close to a newborn's real count, because they counted teeth, cartilage and unfused pieces.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the frame, the armour and the blood factory at once.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half your bones are in your hands and feet.

spotlights.name: Stapes, the smallest bone
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny bone shaped exactly like a stirrup, small enough to sit on a fingertip with room to spare.
spotlights.story_md: The **stapes**, Latin for stirrup, is about **3 millimetres** long and weighs a few milligrams. It is the last of three tiny bones in the middle ear, after the hammer (malleus) and anvil (incus). Together they pass sound from the eardrum to the fluid-filled inner ear, and because the eardrum is much bigger than the oval window the stapes presses on, the chain multiplies the pressure about **20 times**. Without that, most sound would bounce off the fluid like light off water. Two of the three ear bones evolved from bones that formed the jaw joint in ancient reptile-like ancestors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why you can hear a whisper.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your smallest bone is a stirrup that amplifies sound twentyfold.

sections.title: Pump and bellows: heart, blood, lungs
sections.intro_md:
Every cell needs oxygen and must get rid of carbon dioxide. Two systems do it together. The **respiratory system** brings air close to blood. The **circulatory system** carries blood to every cell and back.

The heart is really **two pumps** side by side. The right side sends blood a short way through the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side, with a wall about three times thicker, sends it round the whole body. At rest the heart moves about **5 litres a minute**, the entire blood supply, and up to five times more in hard exercise. It beats about **100,000 times a day** and roughly **3 billion** times in a long life, setting its own rhythm with a cluster of pacemaker cells. No nerve tells it to start.

The lungs are a branching tree of airways ending in about **480 million alveoli**, tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries. Spread flat, their surface would cover roughly **50 to 75 square metres**. Oxygen crosses a barrier thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre.

spotlights.name: The heart
spotlights.spot_it: A fist-sized, cone-shaped muscle tilted to the left of centre, with thick vessels rising from its top.
spotlights.story_md: The heart has four chambers and four one-way valves; the "lub-dub" you hear through a stethoscope is valves snapping shut. It sits only slightly left of centre, but its strongest part, the left ventricle, points left, so that is where you feel the beat. Its rhythm starts in the **sinoatrial node**, a small patch of self-firing cells in the right atrium. That is why a heart taken out for transplant can keep beating with no nerves attached. Heart muscle cells are hardly replaced: about **1% a year** at 25 and under half a percent by 75, so damage from a heart attack is permanent scar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: When it stops for more than a few minutes, everything stops.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two pumps in one fist, setting their own beat.

spotlights.name: Blood vessels
spotlights.spot_it: Thick, elastic arteries; thin, floppy veins with valves; and capillaries so narrow blood cells pass in single file.
spotlights.story_md: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure and have thick muscular walls. Veins carry it back at low pressure and have valves to stop it flowing backwards, the valves Harvey used to prove circulation. In between are **capillaries**, about **5 to 10 micrometres** wide, with walls one cell thick, where oxygen and food leave the blood. No cell in active tissue is far from one. The total length of all vessels is often quoted as **100,000 km**, more than twice round the Earth. That figure is old and poorly sourced; modern estimates vary widely, and some are much lower.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Capillaries are where circulation actually does its job.
spotlights.memory_hook: The pipes narrow until blood cells walk in single file.

spotlights.name: Alveoli, the air sacs
spotlights.spot_it: Under a microscope: a lacy foam of thin-walled bubbles, each about a fifth of a millimetre across.
spotlights.story_md: In **2004** Matthias Ochs and colleagues counted alveoli in six adult lungs using careful sampling. The average was **480 million**, ranging from **274 to 790 million**, with bigger lungs simply having more. Each air sac is about **0.2 mm** across and wrapped in a net of capillaries. The wall between air and blood is often less than **a micrometre** thick. A film of surfactant, a soapy mix of fat and protein, stops the tiny sacs from collapsing as you breathe out. Babies born very early often lack it, which is why premature birth can mean struggling lungs and why synthetic surfactant has saved so many lives since the 1990s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: This is the only place where oxygen gets into you.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a billion bubbles, kept open by soap.

sections.title: The tube through you: digestion
sections.intro_md:
Topologically, you are a doughnut. The digestive tract is a tube that runs from mouth to anus, and its inside is, strictly, outside your body. Food in it has not yet entered you. It enters only when it crosses the lining.

The tube does four jobs. It **moves** food along with waves of smooth muscle, called peristalsis, which work even upside down: astronauts and people hanging off a bar can still swallow. It **breaks food down**, mechanically by chewing and churning and chemically with acid and enzymes. It **absorbs** the small molecules, mostly in the small intestine. And it **gets rid** of what is left.

Two big glands hang off the tube. The **liver** makes bile to emulsify fat and processes everything absorbed before the rest of the body sees it. The **pancreas** makes most of the digestive enzymes, plus the hormones insulin and glucagon. The colon houses most of your microbes. A meal takes roughly a day or two to make the whole trip.

visual.title: The trip, stage by stage (typical times)

data.what happens: Acid and churning, protein digestion starts

spotlights.name: The stomach
spotlights.spot_it: A J-shaped bag under the left ribs; seen through an endoscope, pink folds called rugae that flatten as it fills.
spotlights.story_md: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid strong enough to reach **pH 1.5 to 3.5**, enough to kill most germs and unfold proteins so enzymes can cut them. It does not digest itself because the lining is coated with a thick layer of alkaline mucus, and the surface cells are replaced every few days. An empty stomach holds only about 50 to 100 ml but stretches to take a litre or more. Very little is absorbed here: water, alcohol and some drugs such as aspirin. Most of what you eat leaves the stomach as a soupy mix called chyme, a few spoonfuls at a time.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the acid gate that sterilises and starts digestion.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bag of acid that does not eat itself because it wears a mucus coat.

spotlights.name: Barry Marshall drinks the bacteria
spotlights.spot_it: A photo of a smiling Australian doctor; the experiment itself was a glass of cloudy broth.
spotlights.story_md: In the early 1980s almost every doctor believed stomach ulcers came from stress and acid. **Robin Warren**, a pathologist in Perth, kept seeing spiral bacteria in inflamed stomach biopsies. His young colleague **Barry Marshall** could not make the bacteria infect pigs. So in **1984** he drank a culture of *Helicobacter pylori* himself. Within days he had inflamed stomach lining, vomiting and bad breath, confirmed by biopsy, and he cleared it with antibiotics. It took another decade for treatment to change. Ulcers became curable with a course of antibiotics, and the pair won the **2005** Nobel Prize.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It overturned a medical consensus by self-experiment.
spotlights.memory_hook: To prove his point, he drank the germ.

spotlights.name: Small intestine and its villi
spotlights.spot_it: Under a microscope: a velvet of finger-like villi, each covered in even smaller microvilli, a brush border.
spotlights.story_md: The small intestine is the main site of absorption. Its length is usually given as **6 to 7 metres**, but that is from dead bodies, where the muscle has relaxed. In a living person it is shorter, roughly **3 to 5 metres**. Its lining is folded, the folds are covered with villi about **1 mm** tall, and each lining cell carries thousands of microvilli. Textbooks long said all this gave the gut the area of a **tennis court**. In **2014** Herbert Helander and Lars Fandriks re-measured and found the whole digestive tract has an inner surface of about **32 square metres**, closer to half a badminton court.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The more area, the more food you can absorb.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not a tennis court: about half a badminton court.

spotlights.name: The liver
spotlights.spot_it: A large wedge-shaped, dark reddish-brown organ tucked under the right ribs, the biggest solid organ inside you.
spotlights.story_md: The liver receives all blood from the gut before the rest of the body does, so it is the body's checkpoint: it stores sugar as glycogen, makes blood-clotting proteins and cholesterol, breaks down alcohol and drugs, and turns toxic ammonia into urea. Its most famous trick is regrowth. Remove up to two-thirds and the remainder grows back to roughly the original size within weeks to months. That is what makes **living-donor liver transplants** possible: a healthy adult gives part of their liver to a relative, and both pieces regrow. The Greek myth of Prometheus, whose liver an eagle ate each day and which grew back each night, is an uncanny fit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the chemical factory and filter for everything you swallow.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cut it to a third and it grows back.

spotlights.name: The gut microbiome
spotlights.spot_it: No single look: billions of rods and spheres of hundreds of species, packed most densely in the colon.
spotlights.story_md: Almost all your bacteria live in the **colon**, at densities among the highest of any ecosystem on Earth. Hundreds of species share the space, and each person's mix is different, shaped by birth, diet, antibiotics and age. They ferment fibre that your own enzymes cannot touch, producing short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells of the colon lining. They make vitamin K and some B vitamins and help keep out harmful microbes by taking up space. Links to mood, weight and allergy are an active research field with many striking mouse studies and fewer clear results in people. Faecal transplants are an approved treatment for recurrent *C. difficile* infection.
spotlights.why_it_matters: You are an ecosystem, not a lone organism.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half your cells by count are not you, and they eat what you cannot.

sections.title: Wires and chemistry: brain, nerves, hormones
sections.intro_md:
The body has two control systems. The **nervous system** is fast and precise: electrical signals along nerves, reaching a specific muscle in milliseconds. The **endocrine system** is slow and broad: hormones released into the blood that reach every cell with the right receptor, over minutes to years.

The brain weighs about **1.3 to 1.4 kg**, about **2%** of body weight, yet uses about **20%** of the energy you burn at rest. In **2009** Suzana Herculano-Houzel and colleagues counted its cells by dissolving brains into a uniform soup and counting nuclei: about **86 billion neurons** and about **85 billion** other cells. That killed the old claim of 100 billion neurons and ten glia for every one. Surprisingly, about **69 billion** of those neurons sit in the **cerebellum**, the fist-sized structure at the back that coordinates movement.

The endocrine glands include the pituitary at the base of the brain, the thyroid in the neck, the adrenals above the kidneys and the hormone-making islets of the pancreas.

visual.title: Where the brain's neurons are (billions, approximate)

spotlights.name: The human brain
spotlights.spot_it: A wrinkled, greyish-pink organ about the size of two fists, with a smaller striped structure, the cerebellum, at the back.
spotlights.story_md: The wrinkles fold a large sheet of cortex, about **2 to 4 mm** thick, into the skull; flattened out it would cover roughly the area of a large pillowcase. The outer layer, grey matter, holds the neuron bodies; the white matter inside is the axons, wrapped in fatty myelin. A cut brain shows both clearly. The brain has no pain receptors of its own, which is why some brain surgery is done with the patient awake and talking, so surgeons can test speech as they go. It floats in about **150 ml** of cerebrospinal fluid, which makes it feel much lighter than its weight.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Everything you know and feel is in there.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two percent of your weight, a fifth of your energy.

spotlights.name: Phineas Gage
spotlights.spot_it: An old photograph of a one-eyed man holding a long iron rod.
spotlights.story_md: On **13 September 1848** a railway foreman named **Phineas Gage** was tamping blasting powder when it exploded. His iron rod, about **1.1 metres** long and **6 kg**, shot through his left cheek and out of the top of his head, landing some 25 metres away. He was talking within minutes. His doctor later reported that his personality changed so much friends said he was "no longer Gage". He became the textbook case for the frontal lobes and personality. Later research found he worked for years as a stagecoach driver in Chile, which suggests a large recovery. He died in **1860**. The textbook story was exaggerated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He linked a brain region to character, and shows how case stories grow in retelling.
spotlights.memory_hook: An iron rod through the head, and a man who drove stagecoaches afterwards.

spotlights.name: Henry Molaison, patient H.M.
spotlights.spot_it: A young man in a 1950s photo; for decades known only by his initials.
spotlights.story_md: In **1953** surgeon William Scoville removed parts of both medial temporal lobes, including most of the **hippocampus**, from 27-year-old **Henry Molaison** to stop severe epilepsy. The seizures eased. But he could no longer form new long-term memories. Psychologist **Brenda Milner** found he could still learn a skill, drawing a star while looking in a mirror, getting better each day while never remembering having practised. That split memory into types: facts and events need the hippocampus, skills do not. After he died in **2008**, his brain was cut into **2,401** thin slices and scanned, so researchers can still study it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that memory is not one thing.
spotlights.memory_hook: He learned to draw in a mirror and never remembered learning.

spotlights.name: Pancreatic islets and insulin
spotlights.spot_it: Under a microscope: pale round clusters of cells, like islands, scattered in darker enzyme-making tissue.
spotlights.story_md: The pancreas is mostly an enzyme factory for the gut. Scattered through it are about **1 million** small clusters of hormone cells, the **islets of Langerhans**, together only about **1 to 2%** of the organ. Their beta cells make **insulin**, which lets cells take sugar out of the blood. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys them. In **1921** Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto extracted insulin from dog pancreases, and in **January 1922** a 14-year-old boy, Leonard Thompson, became the first person treated. A disease that killed within months became one you could live with.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A gram or two of tissue controls your blood sugar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Islands of cells, one percent of an organ, keeping you alive.

sections.title: Filters and guards: kidneys and immunity
sections.intro_md:
Staying alive means keeping the inside stable while the outside changes, a balance physiologists call **homeostasis**. Two systems do much of the work.

The **kidneys**, each about the size of a fist and weighing about **150 grams**, receive about a fifth of the blood the heart pumps. They filter about **180 litres** of fluid out of the blood every day, then take almost all of it back, leaving **1 to 2 litres** of urine with the waste, extra salt and water. They also set blood pressure, keep blood at the right acidity, and make the hormone that tells marrow to make red cells.

The **immune system** is a system with no single organ: white cells made in the marrow, trained in the thymus, gathered in lymph nodes and the spleen, and patrolling everywhere. It has a fast, general **innate** arm, including neutrophils and macrophages that eat invaders, and a slow, precise **adaptive** arm of T cells and B cells that learn and remember. Vaccines work by training the second arm in advance.

spotlights.name: Kidney and nephron
spotlights.spot_it: A bean-shaped, dark red organ against the back wall of the abdomen; under a microscope, round tufts of capillaries called glomeruli.
spotlights.story_md: Each kidney holds about **a million nephrons**, the units that do the filtering. A nephron starts with a **glomerulus**, a tight ball of capillaries that leaks fluid into a cup, then runs into a long winding tube that pulls back sugar, salt and water in measured amounts. Your whole blood plasma passes through the filters about **60 times a day**. You can live a normal life with one kidney, which is why living donation is possible. Kidney stones are minerals that crystallise out of urine; Henry Vandyke Carter, the illustrator of Gray's Anatomy, wrote a book on their microscopic structure in Bombay in 1873.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It decides what stays in your blood and what goes.
spotlights.memory_hook: 180 litres filtered a day, and all but one or two given back.

spotlights.name: Neutrophil
spotlights.spot_it: In a blood smear: a pale cell with a nucleus split into three to five lobes, like a string of beads.
spotlights.story_md: Neutrophils make up about **half to 70%** of white blood cells and are the first to arrive at an infection. They squeeze out of capillaries, follow chemical trails to bacteria, and swallow them whole. They can also throw out a sticky web of their own DNA to trap microbes, a trick discovered only in **2004**. They live only hours to a few days, so the marrow makes about **100 billion** a day. **Pus** is mostly dead neutrophils. A famous 1950s film by David Rogers shows one chasing a bacterium around red blood cells like a dog after a rabbit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without neutrophils, a scratch can kill.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pus is a battlefield of dead neutrophils.

spotlights.name: Regulatory T cells
spotlights.spot_it: Under an electron microscope, a T cell is a small round ball covered in short fuzzy projections.
spotlights.story_md: Why does the immune system not attack your own body? Part of the answer is a set of **regulatory T cells** that act as brakes. In **1995** Shimon Sakaguchi in Japan described them. In **2001** Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell in the US found that a mutation in a gene called **FOXP3** caused a deadly autoimmune disease in a mouse strain, and the same gene was behind a rare human disease, IPEX. Sakaguchi then showed FOXP3 controls the brake cells. The three shared the **2025** Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, announced on **6 October 2025**. Treatments that boost or block these cells are in trials for autoimmune disease, transplants and cancer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tolerance of self is as important as attack on invaders.
spotlights.memory_hook: The immune system has brakes, and in 2025 they won a Nobel.

sections.title: More than five senses
sections.intro_md:
Aristotle's list of five senses, sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, is a cultural habit, not a biological count. Your body also senses **balance** (the inner ear's fluid-filled canals), **body position** (stretch sensors in muscles and joints, called proprioception), **temperature**, **pain**, and inner states such as a full bladder or a racing heart, grouped as **interoception**. Depending on how you count, humans have somewhere between about **9 and 20** senses.

Every sense works the same way at heart. A specialised cell turns one kind of energy, light, pressure, chemicals, heat, into electrical signals that nerves carry to the brain. The brain then builds a picture, filling gaps and correcting errors. The eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, and you never notice it because the brain paints over it.

spotlights.name: The eye and retina
spotlights.when: About 126 million light sensors per eye
spotlights.spot_it: Look close at an iris: a ring of coloured fibres and furrows as unique as a fingerprint, around a black pupil.
spotlights.story_md: The retina at the back of each eye holds about **120 million rods**, which work in dim light but see no colour, and about **6 million cones** for colour and detail. The cones crowd into a small central pit, the **fovea**, which is why you move your eyes to read. Oddly, the retina is wired back to front: light passes through the nerve layers before reaching the sensors, and the nerve fibres must exit through the retina, creating the **blind spot**. The lens projects an upside-down image, which the brain turns the right way up. Iris patterns are so individual they are used for ID, including in India's Aadhaar enrolment.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Sight is the sense the human brain spends most on.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your retina is installed back to front, and your brain hides the hole.

spotlights.name: Cochlea and hair cells
spotlights.spot_it: A snail-shell coil, about the size of a pea, buried in the hardest bone of the skull.
spotlights.story_md: The **cochlea** is a coiled tube of fluid, about two and a half turns. Sound vibrations from the stapes ripple the fluid, and a membrane running along the coil vibrates at different places for different pitches: high notes near the base, low notes near the tip. Sitting on it are about **15,000 hair cells** per ear, each topped with a tuft of stiff bristles that bend and fire. Humans cannot regrow hair cells, and loud noise breaks them, which is why hearing loss from concerts and headphones is permanent. Birds can regrow theirs, and researchers are trying to learn how.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hearing depends on a few thousand cells that never come back.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pea-sized snail turns sound into a piano keyboard.

spotlights.name: How many smells can you tell apart?
spotlights.spot_it: No image of a smell: just a nose, and about 400 kinds of smell receptor at the top of it.
spotlights.story_md: In **2014** a paper in *Science* by Caroline Bushdid and colleagues reported that humans can tell apart more than **1 trillion** smells, far more than the old figure of 10,000. It made headlines worldwide. In **2015** Richard Gerkin and Jason Castro showed that the estimate depended heavily on the maths used: small changes in assumptions moved the answer by many orders of magnitude, so the number of smells we can discriminate is still unknown. What is solid: humans have about **400** working smell receptor genes, and our sense of smell is better than its reputation; people can follow a chocolate scent trail across a field on hands and knees.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A great headline number can rest on a fragile calculation.
spotlights.memory_hook: A trillion smells, or maybe not: the maths was the weak spot.

sections.title: India and the study of the body
sections.intro_md:
India's link to anatomy runs from an ancient surgical text to a modern genome project. The **Sushruta Samhita**, compiled over centuries around the turn of the common era, is one of the earliest texts to tell students to learn anatomy from a corpse, and it describes rebuilding a nose with a flap of skin. That technique reached Europe in **1794** through a report from near Pune, and became the root of modern plastic surgery.

Modern anatomy arrived with colonial medical colleges. In **1836** **Madhusudan Gupta** in Calcutta became the first Indian known to dissect a human body in a Western-style medical course, breaking a strong caste taboo. The illustrator of **Gray's Anatomy**, **Henry Vandyke Carter**, spent thirty years teaching anatomy in Bombay. Indian scientists then made discoveries at the heart of cell biology: **Yellapragada Subbarow** helped find the role of ATP in muscle, and **Har Gobind Khorana** helped crack the genetic code. In **January 2025** India released data from about **10,000** genomes sequenced under the GenomeIndia project.

spotlights.name: Sushruta Samhita
spotlights.when: Last centuries BCE to early centuries CE
spotlights.spot_it: Usually shown today as a seated sage with surgical tools; the text itself survives in palm-leaf and paper manuscripts.
spotlights.story_md: The **Sushruta Samhita** is a Sanskrit text on medicine and surgery, compiled in layers from roughly the last centuries BCE into the early centuries CE. It tells surgeons to learn anatomy from a dead body, and later accounts describe the method: the body placed in a cage in a stream for about a week, then the softened layers gently rubbed away with brushes of grass to reveal what lay beneath. It counts **300 bones**, describes dozens of instruments, and gives detailed methods for repairing noses, ears and lips with flaps of skin. Its traditional link to Varanasi comes from later tradition, not firm evidence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest systematic surgical texts in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Learn the body by peeling it, layer by layer, after a week in a river.

spotlights.name: The Indian nose, 1794
spotlights.spot_it: A late eighteenth-century engraving of an Indian man's face with a rebuilt nose and the forehead scar it came from.
spotlights.story_md: **Cowasjee** was a bullock-cart driver with the British army in the war against Tipu Sultan. Captured in **1792**, he had his nose and a hand cut off. About a year later, near Pune, a local practitioner rebuilt his nose using a flap of skin from his forehead, twisted down and stitched into place. Two British surgeons watched, and in **October 1794** a letter in London's *Gentleman's Magazine* described the operation with an engraving. In **1814** Joseph Carpue in London used the "Indian method" on a British officer, and it spread across Europe. Forehead flap reconstruction is still used today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Modern plastic surgery took a key technique from Indian practice.
spotlights.memory_hook: A forehead flap turned down to make a nose, and Europe copied it.

spotlights.name: Madhusudan Gupta
spotlights.spot_it: A nineteenth-century portrait of a Bengali physician; and the colonnaded front of Calcutta Medical College.
spotlights.story_md: In upper-caste Hindu society of the 1830s, touching a corpse was deeply polluting. **Calcutta Medical College**, founded in 1835, needed students to dissect. **Madhusudan Gupta**, a teacher from a family of Ayurvedic physicians, agreed, following Professor Henry Goodeve into a locked storeroom with four students. The date is usually given as **10 January 1836**, though some sources say October. Stories that Fort William fired a **50-gun salute** to mark the day are often repeated but poorly supported. Gupta took sole responsibility to shield his students from backlash. Within a few years, dissection was routine in Indian medical colleges.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It opened modern medical training to Indians.
spotlights.memory_hook: A locked storeroom in Calcutta, and a taboo broken by one teacher.

spotlights.name: Henry Vandyke Carter
spotlights.spot_it: The precise, unshaded line drawings of Gray's Anatomy, labels written right on the structures: that is his hand.
spotlights.story_md: Gray's Anatomy is named after **Henry Gray**, but its famous drawings are by **Henry Vandyke Carter**, who drew them in **1856 to 1857** in his mid twenties, for ten pounds a month. Gray took most of the credit and the royalties. In **1858**, the year the book came out, Carter joined the Indian Medical Service and spent about **30 years** in Bombay, as professor of anatomy and later principal of **Grant Medical College**. There he studied leprosy, mycetoma (once called Madura foot) and relapsing fever. Gray died in 1861 at 34; the book, in its 40-plus editions, has never been out of print.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous anatomy book's images were drawn by a man who built his career in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gray wrote it; Carter drew it, then left for Bombay.

spotlights.name: Yellapragada Subbarow
spotlights.spot_it: A portrait of a bespectacled man in a suit; India issued a postage stamp in his honour.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Bhimavaram** in present-day Andhra Pradesh, **Yellapragada Subbarow** went to Harvard in the 1920s. With Cyrus Fiske he found **phosphocreatine** and showed the part **ATP** plays in muscle, published in **1929**: the energy currency that every cell in this day's story spends. Harvard did not give him a permanent post. At Lederle Laboratories he then led work that produced a way to make **folic acid**, the cancer drug **methotrexate**, and the antibiotic chlortetracycline, discovered by Benjamin Duggar in his department. He died in New York in **1948**, aged 53, little known outside science.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of how cells use energy was worked out with his help.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Bhimavaram to the molecule that powers every cell.

spotlights.name: Har Gobind Khorana
spotlights.spot_it: A black-and-white photo of a smiling scientist from the 1960s; Nobel portrait style.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **1922** in Raipur, a village in Punjab now in Pakistan, **Har Gobind Khorana** studied in Lahore and Liverpool. At the University of Wisconsin he built long chains of RNA with known repeating sequences and used them to work out which three-letter codes, **codons**, stand for which amino acids. That helped complete the **genetic code**, the dictionary every one of your cells uses to turn DNA into protein. He shared the **1968** Nobel Prize with Marshall Nirenberg and Robert Holley. In **1972** his lab made the first artificial gene. He was the third person of Indian origin to win a Nobel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He helped decode the language written in every cell.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three letters, one amino acid: Khorana read the dictionary.

sections.title: Myths about the body, checked
sections.intro_md:
The body is full of facts that everyone knows and that are not true. Most started as a real observation, got simplified, and then were repeated so often that nobody checked. A few began as honest mistakes in scientific papers. The useful habit is to ask of any body fact: who counted, and how?

The ten-to-one bacteria ratio came from one back-of-envelope estimate. The tongue map came from a mistranslated graph. The seven-year rule came from nowhere in particular. The table below lists the common ones; the spotlights take apart three of the most stubborn.

data.myth: We use only 10% of our brains
data.fact: Scans show activity across the whole brain over a day; damage almost anywhere causes problems

data.myth: Different parts of the tongue taste different things
data.fact: All taste qualities are detected all over the tongue

data.myth: Every cell is replaced every seven years
data.fact: Turnover ranges from days to never

data.myth: Bacteria outnumber your cells ten to one

data.fact: It is dark red; veins look blue because of how skin scatters light
Between about 9 and 20, depending on how you count

data.myth: Hair and nails keep growing after death
data.fact: Skin dries and shrinks back, making them look longer

spotlights.name: The 10% brain myth
spotlights.spot_it: Usually spotted in film plots where a pill unlocks the other 90%.
spotlights.story_md: No one knows exactly where the claim began. It is often pinned on the psychologist **William James**, who wrote around 1907 that people use only a small part of their mental resources, which is a statement about effort, not brain tissue. Self-help writers turned it into a number. The evidence against is overwhelming. Brain scans show activity across the whole brain over the course of a day. The brain uses about **20%** of the body's energy; evolution would not keep an organ that costly if 90% sat idle. And there is no region that can be damaged without some effect.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a vague line becomes a precise false number.
spotlights.memory_hook: If 90% were idle, a stroke there would do nothing. It never does nothing.

spotlights.name: The tongue map
spotlights.spot_it: The school diagram: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back, sour and salty at the sides.
spotlights.story_md: In **1901** the German scientist **David Hanig** measured how sensitive different parts of the tongue were to each taste. He found small differences in threshold. In **1942** the Harvard psychologist **Edwin Boring** redrew the data in a way that made those small differences look like separate zones, and textbooks turned that into a map. In fact taste buds all over the tongue, and on the palate and throat, respond to every basic taste, including **umami**, the savoury taste first named in Japan in **1908** and confirmed as a separate receptor around 2000. You can test it now: a pinch of salt on the tip tastes salty.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a redrawn graph can mislead generations.
spotlights.memory_hook: Put sugar on the back of your tongue: still sweet.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Anatomy sounds finished. It is not. Three big efforts are redrawing the map.

The **Human Cell Atlas**, started in **2016**, aims to describe every cell type in the body by the genes it uses. In **November 2024** it published more than **45** studies at once, drawing on about **62 million** cells from about **9,100** donors. Connectomics is mapping the brain's wiring one synapse at a time: in **May 2024** a Harvard and Google team published a 3D map of one cubic millimetre of human cortex. And organ replacement is changing: in **2025** a man in the United States lived **271 days** with a gene-edited pig kidney, a record, and the US regulator cleared the first formal trials.

India is part of this. GenomeIndia released data from about **10,000** Indian genomes in **January 2025**, and in **October 2025** the Nobel Prize for medicine went to the discovery of the immune system's brakes.

data.event: 1 cubic mm of human cortex mapped at synapse level
Human Cell Atlas publishes 45+ studies, 62 million cells
GenomeIndia releases data from about 10,000 genomes
Tim Andrews receives a pig kidney at Massachusetts General Hospital
Nobel Prize for regulatory T cells; Andrews's pig kidney removed after 271 days
Andrews receives a human kidney; HCA publishes a liver atlas roadmap

spotlights.name: The Human Cell Atlas
spotlights.spot_it: Its images are coloured dot clouds: each dot a single cell, clustered by which genes it switches on.
spotlights.story_md: Old textbooks listed about **200** human cell types, sorted by how they looked. The **Human Cell Atlas** sorts them by which genes each cell reads, using a technique that sequences the RNA of single cells. That splits familiar types into many subtypes and finds cells nobody had named. The consortium has more than **3,600** members in about **100** countries. Its **November 2024** package in *Nature* journals included atlases of the gut, the developing skeleton, the placenta and more. The goal is a reference map of a healthy body, so that disease can be read as a change from it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is building the parts list for medicine.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not 200 cell types: hundreds more, sorted by what they read.

spotlights.name: One cubic millimetre of brain, mapped
spotlights.spot_it: A rainbow tangle of neurons, each in its own colour, reconstructed from electron microscope slices.
spotlights.story_md: A tiny piece of temporal cortex, removed during epilepsy surgery, was cut into about **5,000** slices, each about **30 nanometres** thick, and imaged with an electron microscope. Google's software traced every cell. The result, published in *Science* in **May 2024** by Alexander Shapson-Coe, Jeff Lichtman and colleagues, held about **57,000 cells** and **150 million synapses** in a sample the size of half a grain of rice, and took about **1.4 petabytes** of data. It turned up surprises, such as single axons making dozens of contacts on one neuron. A whole human brain at this detail is still far beyond reach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how much wiring sits in a speck of brain.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a grain of rice of brain filled 1.4 petabytes.

spotlights.name: Pig kidneys in people
spotlights.spot_it: A hospital photo; the kidney itself looks like a human one, but comes from a pig with dozens of gene edits.
spotlights.story_md: More than 90,000 people in the US alone wait for a kidney. Pigs have kidneys of the right size, but the human immune system attacks them. Companies such as eGenesis and United Therapeutics edit pig genes, removing pig sugars that trigger attack and adding human genes. In **March 2024** Richard Slayman became the first living person to receive one, at **Massachusetts General Hospital**. In **January 2025** Tim Andrews got one there, came off dialysis, and kept it for **271 days**, more than double the previous record, before it was removed in **October 2025**. In **January 2026** he received a human kidney. Formal trials are now cleared.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It could end the organ shortage, if rejection can be beaten.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pig kidney, human patient: 271 days and counting up.

spotlights.name: GenomeIndia
spotlights.spot_it: No single image: it is a database of DNA sequences from people across India's many communities.
spotlights.story_md: Most genome research has been done on people of European descent, so medicine knows less about which variants matter in Indians. **GenomeIndia**, launched in **2020** by the Department of Biotechnology with about 20 institutions, set out to sequence at least **10,000** Indians from many population groups. In **January 2025** the data from about **10,000** genomes was released for researchers through the Indian Biological Data Centre. It is meant to help find disease variants that are common in India but rare elsewhere, and to make genetic tests fit Indian patients. Next phases aim far larger.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One body plan, many genetic dialects: medicine needs them all.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten thousand Indian genomes to read the local dialect of DNA.

sections.title: Recap: the ladder, top to bottom
sections.intro_md:
The whole tour fits on one ladder. **Cells** are the smallest living units, about 30 to 37 trillion of them, most of them red blood cells, each with a nucleus of plans (except the red ones), mitochondria for power, and a membrane for a wall. Cells of a kind form the **four tissues**: epithelium covers, connective tissue supports, muscle moves, nervous tissue signals. Tissues combine into **organs**, such as the heart, liver and skin, and organs team up as **11 systems**.

The body is not fixed. About 330 billion cells are replaced each day, yet your cortex neurons are as old as you. Its inventory is still being revised: cell counts in 2016, alveoli in 2004, gut area in 2014, new cell types every year. And the people who mapped it range from Galen with his monkeys to a Calcutta teacher in a locked storeroom and a Kyoto lab with four genes.

If you keep one thing: **structure explains function**. A red cell is a disc to carry oxygen, alveoli are thin to pass gas, villi are folded to absorb. Look at a shape and ask what it is for.

best_facts.fact: About 84% of your human cells, by count, are red blood cells, yet they make up only a small share of your weight.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most of you, by count, is one tiny cell type.

best_facts.fact: You replace about 330 billion cells a day, about 3.8 million a second, mostly blood and gut lining.
best_facts.why_surprising: You are rebuilt faster than you can count.

best_facts.fact: Fallout from 1950s nuclear tests acts as a birth certificate for human cells, showing many cortex neurons are as old as the person.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Cold War side effect became a biology clock.

best_facts.fact: Barry Marshall drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to prove bacteria cause stomach inflammation, and won a Nobel for it.
best_facts.why_surprising: A doctor infected himself to change medicine.

best_facts.fact: Henrietta Lacks's cells, taken without consent in 1951, are still dividing in labs around the world.
best_facts.why_surprising: One woman's cells outlived her by seventy years.

best_facts.fact: Bacteria do not outnumber your cells ten to one; the ratio is about 1.3 to 1, and one bowel movement can tip it.
best_facts.why_surprising: A famous number was off by nearly tenfold.

best_facts.fact: About 69 of the brain's 86 billion neurons are in the cerebellum, not the wrinkled cortex.
best_facts.why_surprising: The thinking cortex is the minority.

best_facts.fact: Your mitochondria are descendants of bacteria, still carry their own DNA, and come almost entirely from your mother.
best_facts.why_surprising: Part of every cell was once a separate creature.

best_facts.fact: The drawings in Gray's Anatomy were made by Henry Vandyke Carter, who then spent about 30 years teaching anatomy in Bombay.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's most famous anatomy images have an Indian chapter.

best_facts.fact: Europe's forehead-flap nose repair came from a 1794 report of an operation near Pune on a man named Cowasjee.
best_facts.why_surprising: A key plastic surgery technique travelled from India to London.

best_facts.fact: A cubic millimetre of human cortex, half a grain of rice, held 57,000 cells and 150 million synapses and filled 1.4 petabytes of data.
best_facts.why_surprising: A speck of brain outweighs most hard drives.

best_facts.fact: Patient H.M. learned to draw in a mirror, improving daily, while never remembering he had practised.
best_facts.why_surprising: Memory is several systems, not one.

best_facts.fact: The gut's inner surface is about 32 square metres, roughly half a badminton court, not the tennis court of textbooks.
best_facts.why_surprising: A textbook favourite was out by about ten times.

best_facts.fact: A newborn has about 270 to 300 bone pieces; an adult has 206. The Sushruta Samhita counted 300.
Vesalius's muscle-man woodcuts, laid side by side, form one continuous Italian landscape.
best_facts.why_surprising: An anatomy book hides a panorama.

best_facts.fact: Your heart starts each beat by itself; a heart removed for transplant keeps beating with no nerves attached.
best_facts.why_surprising: The heart does not wait for the brain.

best_facts.fact: The tongue map comes from a 1942 redrawing of a 1901 graph; every taste is sensed all over the tongue.
best_facts.why_surprising: A school diagram was a drawing error.

best_facts.fact: A man lived 271 days with a gene-edited pig kidney in 2025, more than double the previous record.
best_facts.why_surprising: Organ supply may come from farms.

side_dish.title: Leonardo's secret anatomy
side_dish.body_md:
Around **1507 to 1513**, Leonardo da Vinci dissected roughly **30 human bodies**, in hospitals in Florence, Milan and Rome, often at night and by candlelight, before refrigeration. He drew what he found with a precision no one would match for decades: the curves of the spine, the layers of muscle in the shoulder, a foetus curled in the womb, and the heart.

His heart drawings hold a remarkable insight. Leonardo built a glass model of the aorta, poured water with grass seeds through it, and watched swirls form behind the valve's three cusps. He concluded the swirls help the valve close. Modern MRI studies of blood flow have confirmed that such vortices exist and play a role.

Yet his anatomy changed almost nothing. He never published it. The notebooks passed to his pupil Francesco Melzi, then were scattered, and most of the anatomical sheets ended up in the **Royal Collection** at Windsor, where they were not widely studied until the late 1800s and 1900s. Vesalius, who did publish, got the credit for founding modern anatomy in 1543.

The lesson for anyone who makes things: a discovery that stays in a drawer does not count for much. Vesalius's woodcuts, printed and copied across Europe, changed medicine. Leonardo's drawings, better in places, waited four hundred years for an audience.

offline_task.title: Three experiments on your own body
offline_task.body_md:
**1. Count your heart.** Put two fingers on the side of your neck, just under the jaw. Count beats for 30 seconds and double it. Multiply by 60 and by 24. That is roughly how many times your heart will beat today. Most adults land between 85,000 and 115,000.

**2. Find your blind spot.** On a piece of paper, draw a small cross and, about 8 cm to its right, a dot. Close your left eye, look at the cross with your right eye, and slowly bring the paper towards your face. At about 25 to 35 cm, the dot vanishes. That is where your optic nerve leaves the retina. Notice that the brain fills the gap with plain paper.

**3. Kill the tongue map.** Dab a little salt, then sugar, on the very tip, then the sides, then the back of your tongue, rinsing between. Every taste shows up everywhere.

Write down your heart number. Tomorrow, check it again after climbing stairs.
